title: Marriage to an Indian Citizen Gives No Right to Stay, Delhi High Court Rules
excerpt: Dismissing a US citizen's plea to convert her tourist visa into an X-1 spouse visa, Justice Amit Mahajan held that a foreigner's entry and stay are matters of sovereign discretion — and that a marriage certificate does not stop authorities from examining the circumstances.
body:
• The Delhi High Court has held that marriage to an Indian citizen does not, by itself, give a foreign national an automatic or indefeasible right to convert a visa into an Entry (X-1) spouse visa or to stay in India.
  • Justice Amit Mahajan dismissed the plea of US citizen Lisa Hall Srivastava, accepting the immigration authorities' explanation that their suspicion of a marriage of convenience was well-founded on the circumstances on record.
  • The court stressed that it had not adjudicated the validity or genuineness of the marriage, and that any representation she files must still be decided by the authorities in accordance with law.
  • For foreign spouses of Indian citizens, the ruling means an X-1 application is decided on its merits: marriage is the basis for applying, not a guarantee of approval, and officials may examine the marriage's surrounding circumstances.

Marrying an Indian citizen does not give a foreign national a right to live in India. The Delhi High Court made that clear this week, dismissing a US citizen's petition to convert her e-Tourist Visa into an Entry (X-1) spouse visa and holding that the entry and continued stay of foreigners in India are matters of sovereign discretion, not enforceable rights against the State.

The case

The petitioner, Lisa Hall Srivastava, married Mohd. Wasim Akram on December 7, 2025, in accordance with Muslim rites and customs; the marriage was subsequently solemnised before a Marriage Officer under the Special Marriage Act, 1954, on March 18. She told the court that the Foreigners Regional Registration Office (FRRO) had not favourably processed her visa conversion despite the documents she submitted, and that she and her husband had faced repeated enquiries on account of the age difference between them. She also sought protection against deportation or coercive action, a personal hearing in the presence of her advocate, and compensation of Rs 5 lakh for alleged harassment and financial losses, according to ANI's report of the proceedings.

The Centre's counter-affidavit set out a longer history. The petitioner had earlier married an OCI cardholder and obtained OCI status on that basis; that marriage was dissolved in July 2021 and her OCI status was cancelled in November 2023. A second marriage, solemnised in December 2022, ended in November 2025, and her applications for visa conversion and extension on that basis had not succeeded because of deficiencies in supporting documents. The authorities also pointed out that she had been living as a tenant in premises owned by her present husband even before their marriage, and that he had accompanied her during the period when she was pursuing immigration benefits on the basis of her previous marriage. Taking the circumstances together — successive matrimonial relationships, a prolonged stay in India, previous attempts to secure immigration benefits through marriages, residential arrangements and explanations of income — the competent authority had formed a prima facie opinion that the present marriage could be a marriage of convenience, and that a financial or contractual arrangement to facilitate immigration benefits could not be ruled out.

What the court held

"The mere fact that the Petitioner has entered into a marriage with an Indian citizen does not, by itself, confer an automatic or indefeasible right to conversion of her existing visa into an Entry (X-1) Visa."

— Justice Amit Mahajan, Delhi High Court

Accepting the authorities' explanation, Justice Mahajan observed: "This Court finds that the explanation furnished by the Respondents in the Counter Affidavit is satisfactory and the suspicion is well-founded." Referring to the Immigration and Foreigners Act, 2025, the court said the grant, conversion and extension of visas, and the regulation of foreign nationals' stay, fall within the domain of the competent authorities. It relied on the Supreme Court's judgment in Louis De Raedt v. Union of India, which held that the fundamental rights available to a foreigner are confined to Article 21 — life and personal liberty — and do not include the Article 19(1)(e) right to reside and settle in India, which is available only to citizens. It also relied on its earlier decision in Randa Chehab v. Union of India, reiterating that a foreign national's entry or stay is not an enforceable right against the State.

Two limits in the judgment matter. First, a marriage certificate does not shield an application from scrutiny: its issuance under the Special Marriage Act does not prevent the immigration authority from examining the circumstances surrounding the marriage and the applicant's eligibility. The court noted that the husband had filed no affidavit corroborating the petitioner's account of the relationship and cohabitation — a relevant circumstance, it said, though not one that by itself determines genuineness. Second, the court expressly did not decide whether this marriage is genuine. Its observations, Live Law reported, were confined to the claim for immigration benefits, and it directed that any representation already pending, or filed in future, be decided by the authorities in accordance with law. The court also declined to substitute its own assessment for the competent authority's in a matter concerning the admission of a foreign national.

What this means for foreign spouses

The ruling is aimed at one specific claim: that marriage, by itself, compels a visa conversion. It does not cancel any existing visa, and it does not bar foreign spouses of Indian citizens from applying. What it confirms is how those applications are decided — by the FRRO and the competent authority on the facts of the case, including the applicant's immigration history and the circumstances of the marriage, rather than automatically on production of a marriage certificate. For diaspora families, where one spouse is a foreign citizen and the couple plans to live in India, the practical lesson is documentary: expect the application to be examined on its merits, and expect prior immigration history to be part of that examination. A fresh representation remains open to applicants whose conversion is refused, and the court has directed that such representations be decided in accordance with law.

nri_angle: Many diaspora families include a foreign-citizen spouse; the ruling confirms that marriage to an Indian citizen is grounds to apply for an X-1 visa, not a right to one.
